items.title: Anthropic S-1: the lab became a business — but growth is slowing
items.idea: Azeem reads the S-1 as proof Anthropic is a business with cash flow and a war chest, not a lab, and 'can become reliably profitable'. Growth is very high but slowing; over 80% of current revenue comes from models six months old or less, so new releases are what re-ignite it. A marginal Q3 loss is possible because of payments to its foundation. Open question: can growth pay for the compute already promised.
items.angle: The bear case moves from 'is AI real' to 'does growth outrun compute commitments'. That is a duration problem, and it prices differently from a demand problem.
items.tweetA: 80% of revenue from models under six months old means the product has a half-life. Anthropic isn't selling software, it's selling a release cadence. Value the cadence, not the ARR.
items.tweetB: The AI bubble debate just changed question. It's no longer 'do customers pay?' (they do) but 'does growth decelerate faster than the compute take-or-pay schedule?' That's a lease-duration trade, not a demand trade. $CRWV $NBIS

charts.desc: Companion AI Investment Brief has 39 charts on the S-1 across six questions. Charts inside, worth opening.

items.title: Customer concentration 'not a major issue' in the Anthropic filing
items.idea: Azeem's EV-member read flags concentration as a non-issue and focuses on where demand is real, how economics are changing and what constrains the next phase. The constraint he names is the ability to fund promised compute, not demand. He also notes the foundation payments could tip Q3 into marginal loss.
items.angle: Concentration was the standard S-1 bear point; if it is a non-issue the debate shifts entirely to the capex ledger.
items.tweetA: Everyone hunted for customer concentration in the S-1 and came back empty. The risk sits on the other side of the ledger: who is on the hook for the compute.
items.tweetB: The Anthropic S-1 killed the demand bear case in one document. What survives is a financing question: promised compute vs growth that is decelerating. Different risk, different instruments, and probably different equities.

items.title: Anthropic's post-IPO governance: one Class F share = 50.1% of votes
items.idea: Seven co-founders form a Founder LLC that casts a single Class F share carrying 50.1% of the vote on key matters. The LTBT elects 4 of 7 directors; Class F and Class A elect the other 3 with F controlling. Shareholders can bypass the trustees: for the first 3 years it needs the Founder LLC plus simple majorities of employee and Class A votes, and the trust's Class T share can be redeemed for nothing. The one route the filings do not close is amending the trust agreement itself.
items.angle: Dual-class plus a purpose trust is a governance structure with no precedent at this market cap. Index inclusion and passive demand questions follow.
items.tweetA: Anthropic IPO governance in one line: seven people hold 50.1% of the vote via one share, four of seven directors come from a trust, and public shareholders can still redeem the trust's share without its consent. Read the amendment paths before the safety-premium narrative.
items.tweetB: If you want to own the 'safety company', the filing tells you what you're buying: a controlled company, a trust that holds a veto in name, and a failsafe that lets a supermajority instruct it. Is that a moat or a discount-to-peers structure? Index providers will have to answer first. $ANT

items.title: Right-sizing memory: does HBM demand survive specialised inference?
items.idea: Memory is now half or more of an accelerator's BOM and customers talk about 'despeccing'. Chipstrat says Micron answered the wrong question: bigger memory helps, but the point is right-sizing per workload. Google's TPU 8i (inference) has less compute and more memory, 8t (training) less memory bandwidth; AMD MI455X carries 432GB HBM4 vs Rubin at 288GB; Rubin CPX uses 128GB GDDR7 with no HBM. HBM takes ~3x the wafers per bit of DDR5, so bits moving to GDDR/LPDDR free wafers.
items.angle: The memory thesis has to be modelled by accelerator architecture and mix, not total bits. Mix shift may even help margin since HBM earns lower margin than other DRAM today.
items.tweetA: The HBM bull case assumes every accelerator wants the max spec. Prefill is compute-bound, decode is memory-bound, KV cache can live in HBM, SRAM or LPDDR. Memory demand is now an architecture forecast.
items.tweetB: Positron's Asimov ships 288GB to 2.3TB of LPDDR5X per chip with zero HBM. If one HBM bit moving to LPDDR frees ~3 wafers' worth of capacity, which memory vendor is long that trade and which one is short it? $MU $000660.KS

charts.desc: Google TPU 8i vs 8t memory/compute comparison likely in article.

items.title: Custom HBM base dies: who captures the value?
items.idea: Micron now co-designs custom base dies with customers starting at HBM4E, so customers put their own logic into the stack. Chipstrat teases a second question on whether that helps or hurts Micron's margins. Micron says the HBM trade ratio only increases with future generations.
items.angle: Custom HBM turns a commodity into a design-in product but hands the logic die value to the customer.
items.tweetA: Custom base dies are the first time a DRAM vendor sells part of its product's brain to someone else. Does that raise switching costs or give the value away?
items.tweetB: Commodity DRAM becomes a co-designed part at HBM4E. In every past case where a supplier lets the customer own the logic layer, the margin migrated to the customer. Micron says the opposite. Watch gross margin on HBM4E, not bit growth. $MU

items.title: The Supercycle: follow the capex, not the winners
items.idea: Dayan says the Anthropic S-1 should put 'peak AI capex' fears to rest: margin per token is elevated and revenue per dollar of compute is rising, and token usage picked up after the latest model, which post-dates the S-1 period. His point: if a large neocloud like CoreWeave went bankrupt tomorrow, its data centres would be bought for pennies and the cycle would continue. He built a data-center tracker that converts project timelines into labour, commodity and compute needs, to time NFP and commodity exposure.
items.angle: Asset-level view of the cycle: bankruptcies recycle the physical assets. Mapping DC online dates to jobs and commodity demand is a tradeable calendar.
items.tweetA: Neocloud bankruptcy doesn't end the capex cycle, it reprices the assets and the next owner runs them cheaper. That's the 2000 fibre playbook. The equity loses, the buildout doesn't.
items.tweetB: A DC tracker that maps online dates to jobs, copper and power draw is a macro calendar nobody else has. If projects land through year-end as he says, where does it show up first: NFP construction, or copper? $FCX $VRT

charts.desc: Fejau's S-1 charts (margin per token; revenue per $ of compute) and DC tracker. Charts inside, worth opening.

items.title: Databricks: $7B run-rate, +80% y/y, agents now outnumber humans on the platform
items.idea: Databricks passed a $7B run-rate growing 80% y/y at a $190B valuation; Lakehouse is $1.5B growing 100%+, and Lakebase launched last year and is already past $100M run-rate. Three years ago every interaction was human; today more queries come from agents than people, and 17M+ databases a day are launched by agents. Ali Ghodsi calls the lakehouse the 'System of Record for Agents' (SORA).
items.angle: 17M agent-created databases per day is a unit-of-demand shift for databases: the buyer is software. Same logic should hit Snowflake, MongoDB, and Postgres hosts.
items.tweetA: Databricks says agents spin up 17 million databases a day. Database pricing was built around human admins provisioning a few. What happens to per-seat and per-instance models when the buyer is an agent?
items.tweetB: Two numbers from the same essay: $7B run-rate at +80%, and more queries from agents than humans. Software revenue has historically been seat-based. When the user is an agent, does the seat model break or does consumption pricing win? $SNOW $MDB

items.title: Ontology grounding lifts agent accuracy from ~50% to 84.5%
items.idea: Databricks says AI has a context problem, not an intelligence problem. In its tests, grounding an agent in the company's ontology raised answer accuracy from about 50% to 84.5%. OntoRank ranks which definitions are authoritative by author, usage and recency. METR task length is cited as doubling roughly every seven months, while most firms still won't let AI update Salesforce records.
items.angle: The moat in enterprise AI is the ontology layer, which echoes Karp's 'chips and ontology' line. It supports the Palantir/data-layer thesis and weakens the 'models eat everything' one.
items.tweetA: 34 points of accuracy from context alone, no new model. That's the whole enterprise AI market in one stat: the model is rented, the ontology is owned.
items.tweetB: Karp says value goes to chips and ontology. Databricks measured it: 50% to 84.5% accuracy from grounding. If that holds, the next model upgrade is worth less than a clean data dictionary. $PLTR $DBX

items.title: The second managerial revolution: everyone becomes a manager
items.idea: The essay frames agents as ending the professional managerial class's monopoly on information routing (Burnham, 1941). Coase's transaction cost logic: firms expand until internal coordination costs equal market costs; agents cut both. Dorsey's 'world model' at Block, Nadella's 'human capital and token capital', and Musk's claim that humans-in-the-loop firms will lose all appear. Execution and judgment are complements, so judgment gets more valuable.
items.angle: Labour-market read: demand shifts from executors to specifiers/reviewers, and middle management as information router is the exposed layer.
items.tweetA: Middle management was an information routing protocol. Agents are a better protocol. Burnham saw managers replace owners; this time the routers are replaced by a record.
items.tweetB: Corporate hierarchy was a latency solution. Remove the latency and the org chart is the thing that was priced in. Which sector has the most layers per dollar of revenue? Banks, insurers, government. That's where the first agent-led restructurings land.

items.title: AI SRE: incidents scale with PRs, and PRs doubled
items.idea: Reliability math: incident rate = change rate x failure probability per change. Most tech companies' PR frequency has doubled in a year because of agents, and Rootly data shows pages are up y/y with out-of-hours pages nearly doubled. ResolveAI rebuilt its investigator three times in two years (scripted, single agent, multi-agent investigator/verifier/communicator). Stripe's agent takes 3 minutes for a simple run and 14 for a deep one. Fully autonomous remediation is still not real; triage and silencing pages is.
items.angle: AI-generated code increases the demand for ops tooling and observability, a second-order beneficiary of coding agents.
items.tweetA: Coding agents doubled change rate. Incident rate = changes x failure probability, so unless P halves, pages double. The AI SRE boom is a tax on AI coding productivity.
items.tweetB: Everyone counts the productivity gain from doubling PRs. Nobody nets out the pager. i = c x p: if c doubles, p has to halve just to stand still. Observability and incident tooling is the hidden cost line of the coding-agent boom. $DDOG $PD

charts.desc: Rootly chart: pages up y/y, out-of-hours pages nearly doubled.

items.title: Self-confirmation and context rot: why single-agent investigators failed
items.idea: ResolveAI's single-agent v2 hit 'context rot' on long multi-service incidents (re-requesting data, contradicting itself) and 'self-confirmation': graded its own hypotheses and nearly always confirmed the first. Fix was structurally independent verifier agents. Rootly lets customers opt in to pool scrubbed incident data, a 'Stack Overflow for AI SREs'. Slack is becoming the default human-to-agent channel.
items.angle: Adversarial multi-agent design is becoming the standard reliability pattern. Pooled operational data is a new network effect.
items.tweetA: Agents grading their own homework confirm the first guess. The fix isn't a better model, it's separation of duties. Same lesson as audit, now applied to software.
items.tweetB: An agent that always confirms its first hypothesis is a junior analyst with no risk manager. The fix, an independent verifier with a different model, is how every sell-side desk already works. AI is rediscovering compliance one architecture at a time.

items.title: New founder archetypes in the AI era
items.idea: Chen lists archetypes AI may unlock: solo founders, non-technical founders, domain experts, kids/students, content creators; each with a pro and a con. Historical 'yes' archetypes rotated by era (Stanford PhDs, dropouts, designers, operators) and 'no' lists (no solos, no non-technical, no dentists) may be wrong now. He notes investor consensus on profiles is self-reinforcing at pre-seed where many small checks must align.
items.angle: Venture pattern-matching is a coordination game; when the tech changes, the profile premium reprices. Early signal for who gets funded in 2027.
items.tweetA: The founder-profile rulebook was a by-product of the distribution channel of the day: .edu emails for Facebook, App Store editors for designers. Change the channel and the profile that wins changes.
items.tweetB: Every VC 'no' list (no solo founders, no creators, no domain experts) was calibrated to when code was the bottleneck. If coding stops being the constraint, the first fund that writes the checks the old list refused gets the dispersion.

items.title: Fill the room before you open the front door
items.idea: Two-sided products fail if early users meet an empty room. The League (Amanda Bradford, 2014) pre-gamed launch with small events and only let in 500 hand-picked people. Recruit the first side while still building, so launch-day users feel ownership.
items.angle: Cold-start tactics for marketplaces and social products; useful pattern for invite-only prediction markets and crypto apps.
items.tweetA: Selective scarcity solves the cold-start problem, not the growth problem. 500 hand-picked users beats 50,000 empty-room signups.
items.tweetB: Marketplaces die from empty rooms, not bad products. The League opened to 500 curated people. Which 2026 consumer-crypto launch is still opening to everyone on day one?

items.title: AI changes the economics of cyber warfare; UK tells households to prepare for 3 days
items.idea: UK government advice (updated Oct 22) asks households to prepare for three days of disruption; Fox reports a 90-day independent-operation target for major US bases. NCSC assesses AI raises frequency and intensity of cyber threats through 2027 ('realistic possibility', roughly 50%). Anthropic's September threat report describes AI executing and coordinating parts of attacks, including a suspected Russian actor whose workflow rebuilt tools after detection. Author plans two weeks of resilience on ~£1,000.
items.angle: Grid-resilience, backup power, solar-plus-storage and cyber defence demand get a government-backed floor from preparedness campaigns. Panic buying already visible in UK sales.
items.tweetA: Governments don't tell households to hold three days of supplies for nothing. Also the US wants bases to run 90 days islanded. Resilience is becoming a procurement category.
items.tweetB: Two data points the same week: UK asks citizens for 3-day readiness, US targets 90-day autonomy at bases. One is household, one is military, both are saying the grid is the soft target. Backup power, microgrids and cyber defence are the beneficiaries. $ENPH $FSLR $CRWD

items.title: Self-custody in an outage: keys are yours, the network is not
items.idea: A banking outage does not erase records; Bank of England describes protected backups and clean-room rebuilds, but warns attacks can hit multiple sites and recovery takes time. Self-custody separates control from the institution, but spending still needs an operating network. Holding USDC self-custodied still leaves Circle issuer, reserve and address-blocking risk. Slop Cash funds code maintenance via monthly pools with a 14-day review before payouts.
items.angle: Self-custody narrative gets a resilience angle but the counterparties don't vanish; stablecoin issuer risk is the weak link.
items.tweetA: Self-custody removes the bank, not the dependency. A hardware wallet in a blackout is a key without a broadcast route.
items.tweetB: The self-custody pitch always skips the last mile: you hold the key, but to spend you need power, internet and an operating network. And if the coin is USDC, Circle can freeze the address. 'Not your keys' is half the dependency stack.

items.title: The Quiet Ones: Quadrature at $17.6M revenue per head
items.idea: Quadrature Capital's core UK subsidiary made about $3bn revenue in the year to Jan 2026, +80% y/y, with 169 staff: roughly $17.6M per head, above Jane Street and Hudson River Trading and behind only XTX Markets. Founders came from D.E. Shaw and G-Research. Case study in hedge fund / prop-trading convergence.
items.angle: Prop firms' revenue per head signals how much alpha sits in market-making and cross-asset flow. Also a read on talent competition for quants.
items.tweetA: 169 people, ~$3bn revenue. That's a bank trading desk's output with a team smaller than a mid-size law firm. Market structure is being captured by tiny engineering shops.
items.tweetB: $17.6M revenue per employee at Quadrature vs a bank where the same number is a rounding error. Someone is earning the spread that used to pay for a trading floor. Who funds the other side? Probably the passive flow. $VIRT

items.title: Liquidity slipping while the collateral multiplier is at a record
items.idea: Global liquidity is declining as a stronger dollar and weakening collateral values press down. Record reliance on the collateral multiplier makes the system more fragile; as nominal liquidity falls investors rotate out of global risk assets, most noticeably the US and emerging Asia.
items.angle: Collateral multiplier plus a dollar bid is the classic tightening transmission that equity multiples ignore until it hits repo. Links to China STAR50 selloff and Brazil.
items.tweetA: A record collateral multiplier means liquidity is levered on asset prices. A stronger dollar and lower collateral values turn that multiplier into a headwind.
items.tweetB: Liquidity falling, dollar up, multiplier at a record. That's a system running on collateral values, which is circular: falling prices shrink collateral, which shrinks liquidity, which lowers prices. China STAR50 -40% and Brazil's worst day since 2020 look like the first links. $DXY

items.title: A (qualified) defense of investment bubbles, Part I of III
items.idea: Former Evergreen CIO recounts being 100% early on two bubbles: the 1980s Nikkei, which doubled after he called it overvalued and exceeded 1929 US valuations, and the dot-com Nasdaq, which doubled after he called it too. Series continues tomorrow and Thursday with market implications. Opens with E.O. Wilson: paleolithic emotions, medieval institutions, godlike technology.
items.angle: Pattern: calling a bubble early costs a full doubling. Useful discipline for the AI capex debate.
items.tweetA: Two bubbles, two doublings after the call. Being right on valuation and wrong on timing is the standard outcome, not the exception.
items.tweetB: Nikkei doubled after he said it was overpriced. Nasdaq doubled after he said it was overpriced. Both bubbles ended exactly as he said, after he was wrong by 100%. Now apply that to anyone shorting AI capex on valuation alone.

items.angle: Political-event risk on AI beta one week before the US midterms. Worth opening the original article.

items.tweetB: Everyone is positioned for the AI trade to continue regardless of who wins. One week to the midterms and nobody can say which party regulates compute faster. Cheap hedge or not?

items.title: Gold $3,980 and silver ~$54 supports under test; tax-loss season is early
items.idea: Selling has increased into the last week of October, putting gold's $3,980 and silver's ~$54 supports in focus. Two paths: a false breakdown that traps bears, or a washout to a 'major low'. Producers should show fat Q3 margins but junior PM and copper stocks show depressed volume and valuations. Seasonal trade: buy into November tax-loss selling, hold into Q1.
items.angle: Gold printed ~$4,010 in Mando today, right on the support. Tax-loss seasonal plus margins is a contrarian setup in miners.
items.tweetA: Gold is sitting on $4,010 with the $3,980 support 0.7% below. Producer margins are fat and sentiment is at lows. That is how washouts look.
items.tweetB: Gold at $4,010 vs support at $3,980: a 0.7% buffer. Miners will print huge margins into earnings and the sector is trading like the margins don't exist. Tax-loss season exists for exactly this. $GDX $GDXJ $SLV

items.title: Concorde's children: what 'failed' moonshots leave behind
items.idea: Concorde never recouped its development cost (up to £2.1bn) and was killed by economics and a 2000 crash, but left fly-by-wire, intake control, CFD and structural analysis, titanium welding (via the US SST) and variable-cycle engine research. Ticket cost roughly $66,000 in 2026 money. Argument: judge R&D by spillovers, not direct sales; the US has grown less tolerant of hardware failure.
items.angle: Supersonic is back on the table via military hypersonics and startups; spillover framing applies to today's fusion, SMR and space bets.
items.tweetA: Concorde's balance sheet is a failure; fly-by-wire alone justified it. Measuring moonshots by direct revenue underprices the technology tree they seed.
items.tweetB: Concorde never repaid its £2.1bn. Fly-by-wire, titanium welding and CFD all came from it and now sit on every airliner. We value R&D by what it sold, not what it seeded. Which of today's 'failures' is seeding the next A320?

items.title: A bull-market crypto portfolio built with Claude: buckets, swing rules, watcher agents
items.idea: Six buckets with target sizes; no token above 15% (trim at 20%); swing trades capped at 4% total, 1.5% each, spot only. Cash 10-14%, NFTs targeted at 15%. TAO: ~11% of supply issued yearly against maybe $30M of real subnet revenue; he is trimming. ENA fee switch triggers once USDe's two-week average passes $7.5B (about $4.6B now). Automations: 4am chain snapshots, Monday research agents, push alerts via ntfy.
items.angle: Retail crypto is productising portfolio rules with agents, which reduces overtrading, and flags TAO and ENA catalysts with numbers.
items.tweetA: TAO: 11% annual issuance vs about $30M subnet revenue. The inflation is more than the market's estimate of fundamental revenue. That's the whole thesis in one line.
items.tweetB: ENA's fee switch needs USDe's two-week average above $7.5B, and it's at $4.6B. That's a 63% increase in supply needed for the catalyst to trigger. Meanwhile TAO emits ~11% a year against ~$30M of revenue. Crypto 'catalysts' usually need the thing the token hasn't got. $ENA $TAO

items.title: Operator behaviour: AI agents replace the trader's spreadsheet
items.idea: The author spent 10-15 hours with Claude building a system: daily wallet snapshots valued against bucket targets, weekly NFT bid valuations, trim/stop prices per token, research dossiers per core token and a 'watcher' agent pinging his phone. He says Claude Code is exceeding even his insane expectations after a break since the start of the year.
items.angle: A real retail-adoption signal for agentic tooling in crypto; same workflow is trivially portable to equities.
items.tweetA: The retail crypto trader's edge is moving from information to process. The agent doesn't know more, it just never forgets to sell.
items.tweetB: A crypto trader's biggest enemy is the janky spreadsheet and forgetting to sell. The agent fixes discipline, not alpha. Everyone will have the same discipline soon, so where does the edge go?

items.title: 'Demographics, debt and debasement broke the system' — book out in one week
items.idea: Pal's The Everything Code is out in one week. Thesis: the gap between effort and outcome keeps widening because of demographics, debt and debasement; 2008 was when the system died; the debt refinancing cycle drives liquidity and explains asset prices; crypto and technology are the only assets that reliably clear the debasement hurdle; it ends on what people do when the economy is handed to machines. Email is mostly a pre-order request.
items.angle: A macro-crypto framework hitting retail via a book launch; pre-order rank shapes attention.
items.tweetA: Liquidity as the refinancing cycle of debt is the idea behind half of macro Twitter. If the book hits the charts, it tests whether that framework is consensus now.
items.tweetB: Pal's whole argument: crypto and tech are the only assets that 'clear the debasement hurdle'. Testable: gold at $4,010 tested the same hurdle this year. What's the hurdle rate and which asset has actually cleared it? $BTC $GLD

items.title: China's housing bust in year six: Goldman raises the drag
items.idea: Goldman increased its estimate of property's drag on Chinese growth because construction, land sales and investment have collapsed deeper than expected, after five years of lowering the bar. Beijing's shift away from presales protects buyers but removes a key developer financing source, potentially extending the contraction into the next decade. Falling household wealth and local government finances reinforce each other. Goldman expects the drag to fade partly because property becomes a smaller share, not because demand recovers.
items.angle: Pairs with Mando's China data: property investment -21% y/y, STAR50 -40% in four months, longest equity losing streak ever.
items.tweetA: The drag fades because property gets smaller, not because it recovers. That's not a recovery, that's a denominator effect.
items.tweetB: Property investment -21% y/y, STAR50 -40% in four months, equities on their longest losing streak ever, and Goldman is raising the property drag estimate. Beijing's end-of-presales rule removes developers' main funding. The bottom isn't in because the funding channel is closing. $FXI $KWEB

items.title: Meta to raise up to $95B in equity for AI capex; Nvidia invests $3B in Meta

items.angle: Capex funding is shifting from cash flow to equity and vendor financing: a late-cycle marker in prior capex booms, or just scale.
items.tweetA: Meta needs $95B of equity for capex and its supplier is writing a cheque. Vendor financing is how the last two capex cycles ended.
items.tweetB: Meta raising up to $95B of equity, Nvidia putting in $3B, Nebius borrowing $3.5B against GPUs from Citi. The buildout is now financed by the people selling into it. That's not a bust signal on its own, but it's the structure that amplifies one. $META $NVDA $NBIS

items.title: Hormuz diplomacy: Iran flexible; Russia ramps diesel after US deal; US gas above Biden average
